title: Trump Pardons Former Palm Beach County Commissioner Mary McCarty
description_medium: Donald Trump pardoned Mary McCarty on December 23, 2020, for a federal honest-services fraud conviction tied to her tenure as a Palm Beach County commissioner. McCarty had pleaded guilty in 2009 and received 42 months in prison, three years of supervised release and a $100,000 fine. Prosecutors said she used her public office to benefit herself, her husband and associates in municipal bond dealings.
description_long:
On December 23, 2020, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Mary McCarty, a former Palm Beach County commissioner. The Justice Department’s clemency record identifies her conviction as honest-services fraud and records a sentence of 42 months in prison, three years of supervised release and a $100,000 fine. McCarty pleaded guilty in 2009. Prosecutors said she used her elected position to benefit herself, her husband and associates in connection with municipal bond transactions, including by accepting gifts or gratuities from people doing business with the county commission.

The pardon forgave the federal conviction; it did not erase the historical conduct or alter the underlying case record. The White House announcement named former Florida attorney general Pam Bondi and conservative media executive Christopher Ruddy among those who supported clemency. McCarty is also the sister of Brian Ballard, a prominent Trump fundraiser and lobbyist, a relationship highlighted in congressional oversight reporting about the pardon. These ties are part of the public context around the grant, while the official clemency record establishes the offense and sentence.
evidence_notes: Corrected the date to the December 23, 2020 clemency grant. DOJ’s warrant/index supports the conviction and sentence; contemporaneous reporting describes the bond transactions and gratuities.

title: Trump Pardons Louisville Activist Christopher II X for Federal Drug Convictions
description_medium: On December 23, 2020, Trump pardoned Louisville community leader Christopher II X, formerly Christopher Anthony Bryant, for federal cocaine offenses. The White House linked the convictions to a two-decade period of addiction and described his later youth and community work, including the nonprofit Game Changers. Senator Rand Paul supported the pardon. Kentucky governor Matt Bevin had pardoned his state convictions in 2019; the federal grant addressed the separate federal convictions.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted a full federal pardon to Louisville community leader Christopher II X, formerly Christopher Anthony Bryant, on December 23, 2020. The White House described the federal cases as cocaine offenses committed during a period of addiction that lasted into the late 1990s. After his release from prison, Bryant became a community organizer and led Game Changers, a nonprofit focused on guiding young people toward constructive opportunities. The White House also described his role as a trusted local voice during tensions between police and residents.

Senator Rand Paul and Spalding University president Tori Murden McClure supported the clemency request. Kentucky governor Matt Bevin had granted Bryant a pardon for state crimes in December 2019. Trump’s action concerned the federal cocaine convictions, a legally separate matter. The distinction matters because the earlier state pardon did not itself forgive federal offenses. The available official announcement establishes the date, clemency scope and community context; it does not detail each federal count or the exact sentence, so those specifics are omitted.

title: Trump Pardons Former California Lawmaker Patrick Nolan
description_medium: Trump pardoned Patrick James Nolan on May 15, 2019, for a racketeering conviction stemming from the FBI’s Operation Shrimpscam. Nolan, a former California Assembly Republican leader, had pleaded guilty in 1994 and served 26 months of a 33-month prison sentence. After release, he became a criminal-justice reform advocate and worked with Prison Fellowship. The White House cited his later advocacy and rehabilitation.
description_long:
On May 15, 2019, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Patrick James Nolan, a former Republican leader in the California State Assembly. Nolan had pleaded guilty in 1994 to racketeering charges arising from an FBI undercover investigation known as Operation Shrimpscam, which concerned a proposed bribery scheme involving public officials. The Justice Department’s clemency record lists a 33-month prison term, and Nolan served 26 months before release.

After leaving prison, Nolan became a prominent advocate for criminal-justice reform and worked with Prison Fellowship, including as a senior vice president. The White House announcement presented his post-conviction work and rehabilitation as reasons supporting clemency and noted his advocacy for crime victims. The pardon forgave the federal conviction; it did not erase the historical case or turn the plea into an acquittal. His trajectory from state legislator to federal defendant and later reform advocate is the essential context for the grant.
evidence_notes: Corrected title and focused on the 1994 racketeering case, sentence, and Nolan’s later reform advocacy described by the White House and Prison Fellowship.

title: Trump Pardons Roy McKeever for 1980s Marijuana Conviction

DOJ records a sentence of 12 months in prison and one year of supervised release for using a telephone to facilitate marijuana distribution. The White House said McKeever had been arrested in 1986 while transporting marijuana from Mexico to Oklahoma and had since led a law-abiding life. His case became a frequently cited example in debates over federal marijuana enforcement.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted Roy McKeever a full pardon on July 29, 2019, for a federal conviction arising from marijuana distribution. The Justice Department’s clemency record says McKeever received 12 months in prison and one year of supervised release for using a telephone to facilitate the distribution of marijuana. The White House described his arrest in 1986 while transporting marijuana from Mexico to Oklahoma and said he had remained law-abiding in the years afterward.

McKeever’s case drew attention because the sentence and lasting federal conviction came from conduct involving marijuana, which many states later treated differently under their own laws. A pardon forgives the federal offense but does not erase the conviction from history or change the law that applied at the time. The official clemency materials establish the grant and sentence; the White House announcement gives the account of his arrest and post-conviction life. This context explains why his pardon featured in discussions of clemency for nonviolent drug offenses.
